title: fix(ai): parse current codex exec events and stop pinning a stale codex model list
body:
This PR fixes Codex CLI agent integration: the installed Codex CLI (0.144.6) emits a dotted `item.completed`/`turn.completed`/`turn.failed`/`error` event stream that the exec-output parser didn't understand, so every generation failed with "Codex: no response in output" even on success; the model picker also offered a hardcoded, now-dead model list instead of the CLI's live catalogue. Both are fixed, with a UI notice when a curated fallback list is shown instead of live discovery, and new coverage for the parser/model-list branches.

Closes #1185

## What changed

- `apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/commands/ai_provider/cli_agent/codex.rs` — detect and parse both the legacy `{"msg":{"type":"agent_message"}}` shape and the current dotted event dialect in `parse_stream_line`/`parse_complete`; stop treating `item.updated` as an incremental delta (only terminal `item.completed` now emits `Delta`/`Thinking`/`Error`); add `discover_models` via `codex debug models`, keeping only `visibility: "list"` rows; harden `parse_debug_models` to skip one malformed row instead of dropping the whole list; hedge `reasoning_text`'s array assumption with a fallback to the scalar fields.
- `apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/commands/ai_provider/cli_agent/mod.rs` — `CliAgentBackend::discover_models` (defaults to `None`; only Codex overrides it), and `CliAgentClient::list_models` prefers live discovery, falling back to the curated list and tagging fallback entries `source: "fallback"`.
- `packages/shared/src/ipc/contracts/ai.ts` — add the `source` field to the model-list contract.
- `apps/desktop/src/renderer/lib/ai-providers/provider-meta.ts` — refresh the curated Codex fallback list to the current real model set.
- `apps/desktop/src/renderer/features/ai-settings/CliAgentConfig/index.tsx` — show an i18n'd notice when every discovered model came from the fallback list rather than the CLI's own catalogue, and render a discovered `displayName` when present; notice copy generalized to state the fact rather than imply a transient outage (applies to every non-Codex CLI agent too, since only Codex overrides discovery).
- `packages/translations/src/locales/{en,de}/translation.json` — new/reworded strings for the fallback notice.
- `apps/desktop/src/renderer/features/ai-settings/CliAgentConfig/CliAgentConfig.test.tsx` — coverage for the fallback notice (including non-Codex agents), the discovered-model-with-no-`displayName` label fallback.
- `apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/commands/ai_provider/cli_agent/codex.rs` (test module) — coverage for `reasoning_text`'s summary-array fallback, unknown `item.completed` kinds in both streaming and complete parsing, `parse_complete` capturing an `agent_message` from a lone `item.updated` (the deliberate streaming/complete asymmetry), and `parse_debug_models` dropping only the malformed row.

## Verification

- `AJH_SKIP_CARGO_TEST=1 git push` — the pre-push gate ran `cargo check`, Rust clippy, Rust formatting check, `cargo-deny`, and `cargo-machete`, all clean; only `cargo test` was skipped (`AJH_SKIP_CARGO_TEST=1`, the sanctioned pre-push gate skip for a known host DLL fault) — CI's Rust test job is authoritative for this PR.

title: fix: Codex CLI integration is broken with current Codex versions
body:
## Describe the bug

The Codex CLI integration appears to be outdated in two places:

1. AI Job Hunter shows a hardcoded/stale model list (`gpt-5-codex`, `o4-mini`) instead of models currently available in Codex CLI.
2. Even when Codex runs successfully, AI Job Hunter fails to parse the current `codex exec --json` output and reports `Codex: no response in output`.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure Codex CLI as an AI provider in AI Job Hunter.
2. Open the model selector.
3. Observe that only old models such as `gpt-5-codex` and `o4-mini` are available.
4. Try running a Codex request.
5. The old models may fail as unavailable.
6. When using a working model through Codex CLI, the request completes but AI Job Hunter reports:

   `Codex: no response in output`

Current Codex CLI exposes models such as:

- `gpt-6-astra`
- `gpt-5.6-sol`
- `gpt-5.6-terra`
- `gpt-5.6-luna`
- `gpt-5.5`

## Expected behaviour

- AI Job Hunter should use/discover models available in the installed Codex CLI instead of relying on a stale hardcoded list.
- Current `codex exec --json` output should be parsed correctly.
- The final Codex response should be returned to AI Job Hunter.

## Actual behaviour

- Only outdated Codex models are shown.
- Selecting them may result in unavailable-model errors.
- Current Codex JSONL responses are not recognized and AI Job Hunter reports:

  `Codex: no response in output`

Current Codex CLI emits events such as `item.completed` and `turn.completed`, which may differ from the format currently expected by AI Job Hunter.

## Environment

- **OS**: macOS, Apple Silicon
- **App version**: 0.150.0
- **Ollama version**: N/A
- **Model in use**: Codex CLI (`gpt-5.6-sol` / other currently available Codex models)
- **Codex CLI version**: 0.153.4

## Additional context

The current Codex model selector (`/model`) shows:

- `gpt-6-astra`
- `gpt-5.6-sol`
- `gpt-5.6-terra`
- `gpt-5.6-luna`
- `gpt-5.5`

It may be better to discover the available Codex models dynamically rather than maintaining a hardcoded list.

title: found_jobs has no lifecycle: an unbounded, unclassified pool with no safe curation surface for the app, an agent, or the user
body:
## Summary

`Autopilot.found_jobs` has no lifecycle beyond "discovered." Every job an Autopilot ever finds is kept forever in one unbounded array, with no status model, no bounded/classified view, and no safe way to turn a large accumulated pool into a small trustworthy working set — whether that's the app doing it on its own, an external agent doing it on request, or a human just trying to look at what's been collected.

This is a capability gap, not a single bug, and not a large-corpus-only concern. It shows up as several already-filed symptoms (#1115, #1129, #1135, #1167, #1168) but the underlying cause — an unbounded, unclassified, un-queryable, un-inspectable job store — is untouched by any of them and isn't the subject of any existing issue or ADR. **Any installation with a long-running Autopilot hits this in weeks, at any corpus size** — this issue is about that general capability, not about cleaning up one particularly large pool.

**Verified against `main` @ `37e6ef4` (current as of filing; re-checked in a clean clone, not inferred from an older audit).**

## Evidence

**The pool has no ceiling and no lifecycle field.**
- `found_jobs: Vec<FoundJob>` is embedded directly in the `Autopilot` record, persisted as one flat `autopilots.json` file, loaded whole and rewritten whole on every mutation (`autopilot/mod.rs`).
- `merge_found_jobs` keeps every previously-seen row forever; there is no length cap, no age-based eviction, no retention pass anywhere in it.
- The app's own code already documents the cost this produces: `commands/autopilot.rs:771-773` — *"the union is real CPU work: measured quadratic in the largest title/company block (3.03s at 2000 items, 12.3s at 4000), unbounded because `found_jobs` is never truncated."*
- `FoundJob` carries no status field. The closest proxy, `InteractionRecord{interactionType}`, is a 5-value enum (`viewed | opened | applied | bookmarked | dismissed`) designed for user-facing interactions, not a job's standing in the pool — and it's read back two different, non-equivalent ways depending on the caller (`postings/mod.rs` joins by `job_id`; `commands/autopilot.rs`'s `autopilot_best_matches_blocking` re-derives a `canonical_job_key` from the interaction row's own fields, because `job_id` has no meaning outside the live scrape cache).
- `commands/autopilot/best_matches.rs:2,11` — the cross-autopilot ranked view is explicitly "recomputed on every call" over the full unbounded union, by design (a cluster spanning two autopilots "belongs to no single one of them"). Correct call for correctness; it also means the cost above is paid on every read, growing with the pool, forever.

**This isn't hypothetical — the newest feature already amplifies it.**
- #1114/PR #1117 (merged 2026-09-07) added an automatic background enrichment pass: after every `autopilot_run`, up to 15 blank LinkedIn descriptions get fetched via `scraping::scrape_url::resolve` and written back (`commands/autopilot.rs:663-684`, `autopilot_helpers/linkedin_enrich.rs`).
- That resolver's last-resort fallback, `main_content_text` (`scraping/scrape_url/mod.rs:901`, still present, still wired at line 539), picks the *longest* `<main>`/`<article>` block on the page with no content-quality scoring at all. Against a login-walled or rate-limited response, that block can be the page's own nav/footer chrome — which then gets written into `FoundJob.description` as if it were the real job ad, with no signal distinguishing it from genuine content.
- So as of the current build, corrupted-looking descriptions can now enter the pool **automatically, on every scheduled run**, not just via manual `scrape_resolve_url` calls. There's nowhere in the pipeline that would ever notice.

**No human-facing view of the collected corpus exists either — checked directly, not inferred:**
- `/jobs` (`JobsPage`) is manual scrape + hybrid search over the *ephemeral* `PostingsCache` — it never reads the persisted Autopilot corpus at all.
- `AutopilotCard` renders one autopilot's `found_jobs` into an unpaginated scroll container with no filtering.
- `BestMatchesPage` is a capped top-100 cross-autopilot view, sort-only, no status/quality filters.
- `data_export` (`commands/data.rs`) is a whole-app backup bundle — every store, native save-file dialog, disaster-recovery shaped — not a targeted, browsable, or filterable view of one's own job data.
- Net effect: today, a user cannot see, filter, or export the full set of jobs the app has actually collected about them. This is a real gap in its own right, not just a side effect of the performance problem above.

**What already exists and should be reused, not rebuilt:**
- Automatic fuzzy duplicate clustering already runs on every scrape and every autopilot run — `scraping::cluster::assign_clusters` (block by normalized company + title-first-token, join by trigram-Jaccard ≥ 0.90 or embedding cosine ≥ 0.92), with a tombstone veto for user-corrected false merges (`dedup/mod.rs`). A lifecycle/classification layer should sit on top of this, not duplicate it.
- A working skill-gap engine already exists for exactly "what does this job need vs. what do I have": `commands::match_resume::score_one` — keyword coverage + embedding cosine, a `gaps` list in readable form, cached per `(resume_id, job_id)`.
- A cost-safe batch-AI pattern already exists and is well-designed: `commands/autopilot/rerank.rs` — cheap prefilter first, expensive pass capped at top-N, per-item degrade that never fails the run, a circuit breaker, `charge_provider_daily` billed only on a real round-trip, cache-first so repeat runs cost nothing.
- **The AI layer is already provider-agnostic — this needs preserving, not building.** `ProviderId` already spans `Ollama | OllamaCloud | OpenAi | OpenAiCompatible | Anthropic | Gemini | ClaudeCode | Codex | GeminiCli | Antigravity` (`commands/ai_provider/mod.rs`), where `OpenAiCompatible` alone covers LM Studio/vLLM/OpenRouter/Groq/Together/DeepSeek. Every generation feature resolves through one seam, `Completer::from_active` (`pipeline/mod.rs`), which reads whichever provider `AiConfigStore` currently points at with no hardcoding. `charge_provider_daily(provider: &str, ...)` (`limits/mod.rs:430`) gates spend per-provider, not per-vendor-special-case. Embedding vectors are already tagged `provider`+`model`+`dim` and only compared "same-space" — swapping providers just ages out old vectors and falls back to keyword scoring, it never breaks. Any new maintenance pipeline gets this for free through the same seam; it should not reach for a provider-specific SDK or hardcode any single vendor.
- `scraping/trust/mod.rs:6-9` already states the right philosophy for this: *"V1 is flag-only: enrich, never drop. A low score never removes a posting."* That discipline needs a real state machine to enforce it consistently, not just advisory flags.
- ADR-036 (`docs/knowledge/decision-records/adr-036-cross-autopilot-best-matches.md:133`) already anticipated the interaction-type enum growing — *"a fifth enum member `'dismissed'`... makes future additions similarly obvious"* — a lifecycle status is a natural extension of a pattern the codebase already uses, not a foreign concept.

## Why this doesn't scale

Every Autopilot run only ever adds to `found_jobs`; nothing ever leaves it except a full autopilot deletion. A user running several Autopilots continuously for weeks or months — which is the intended use of a scheduled autopilot, not an edge case — ends up with a pool where:
- Every read that has to reason about the whole pool (clustering, best-matches, any future analysis) gets slower as a function of total-jobs-ever-seen, not active-jobs-now.
- Genuinely dead, corrupted, or irrelevant records sit alongside live ones with no way to tell them apart at a glance or at scale, in the GUI, over the agent surface, or by the app itself.
- The MCP/agent surface has the identical problem one layer up: `found-jobs` pagination (#1115, shipped) and the compact-projection/filter work already scheduled in #1167/#1168 make *reading* the existing unbounded corpus efficient — they don't stop the corpus itself from growing without bound, and they don't give an agent (or the app, or the user) any notion of a job's standing beyond raw fields.

## What already exists, what must be added

**Exists and should be reused as-is** (see Evidence above for citations): automatic dedup/cluster engine · resume skill-gap engine · cost-safe batch-AI pattern (`rerank.rs`) · provider-agnostic AI seam + per-provider budget gating · advisory trust flags · a pagination/filtering convention already being extended in #1167/#1168.

**Genuinely missing:**
1. **A real per-job lifecycle**, distinct from the user-interaction log, that the app, an agent, and the user can all reason about and transition through — something in the shape of *active → needs verification → archived/historical → junk*, illustrative only, not prescriptive.
2. **A bound on pool growth** — whether that's relational storage instead of one growing array, an age/interaction-based retention pass that moves rows out of the "hot" set, or something else the maintainer judges best.
3. **A classification/curation mechanism** that reuses the dedup/cluster engine and the skill-gap engine already in the app, following the same cost discipline `rerank.rs` already established, to keep the *active* pool small and trustworthy — runnable both on a schedule by the app itself and on request by an agent.
4. **A bounded, queryable surface over pool state itself** — not just over raw fields (#1167/#1168 territory) but over questions like "what's a likely duplicate of what," "what looks corrupted," "what hasn't been touched in N weeks," "why is this job in this state."
5. **A human-facing view of the full corpus and its curation state** — today there is none (see Evidence above); this is not automatically solved by fixing the agent surface.

All five items above persist in the app's own data layer. Curation state is not owned by, or reset by, any AI provider, model, API key, or agent session — swapping any of those must leave prior classification and lifecycle decisions intact.

## What the app should do autonomously

The app already uses a configured AI provider for scoring, tailoring, and other tasks; this should extend to periodic self-maintenance without requiring a human or an external agent to repeatedly ask for it. Two different cadences are the natural fit, matching how the app is already structured rather than inventing a new shape:

- **Incremental, per-run classification** for newly-discovered jobs fits naturally as another phase inside `autopilot_run`, alongside the existing opt-in semantic-rerank and AI-notes phases — same cost gating (`charge_provider_daily`), same place in the pipeline. One reasonable reading of the stages involved — `scrape → normalize → dedupe → validate → classify → repair/enrich → reassess → archive/retain → prioritize` — is illustrative, not mandatory, and is mostly an extension of stages `autopilot_run` already has (score → `cluster_aware_retain` → optional rerank → optional AI notes → persist), not new invention.
- **Corpus-wide reassessment** (staleness, cross-autopilot dedup, archival) is inherently cross-autopilot, the same way `best_matches` already unions across all of them — that argues for a fifth scheduler on the existing hand-rolled pattern (`autopilot_scheduler.rs` / `email_watch_scheduler.rs` / `reminder_scheduler.rs`), not something crammed into one autopilot's run.

Whichever shape is chosen, it must degrade gracefully (a provider outage or budget exhaustion pauses AI-assisted classification, it doesn't corrupt or lose state) and must never require a human to be present for the pool to stay maintained.

## What an external agent should be able to do

The long-term goal is for an agent (Claude or otherwise) to act as a safe operator over this data on request — inspecting the pool, finding low-value or corrupted records, repairing what's repairable, moving what shouldn't stay in the active set out of it — without a human manually reading thousands of records to get there. Concretely, within bounded/paged calls, an agent should be able to:

- inspect the shape of the job population (counts by state, by source, by age — not raw rows) without downloading it;
- find likely-duplicate/clustered records and why they were grouped (this already exists internally — it just isn't exposed as reasoning an agent can act on);
- find records that look corrupted or too thin to trust, using signals the app already computes (trust flags, description-availability, the enrichment-fallback risk above);
- find stale or long-untouched records;
- request classification/enrichment of specific records, and repair recoverable ones;
- move a record between lifecycle states with a stated reason, and undo it;
- retrieve a bounded, curated, high-value subset for deeper analysis instead of the entire history;
- ask why a given record ended up in its current state;
- do all of the above incrementally as new jobs arrive, not by re-processing the whole corpus every time.

None of this should require raising the MCP transport/payload cap — that only relocates today's problem instead of resolving it — and none of it should mean silently deleting anything. Every transition should stay inspectable and, wherever practical, reversible.

## What the human user should be able to inspect and control

The user must not be locked out of their own collected data. Whatever ships should let the user:

- see the full corpus the app has collected — not just what fits in an unpaginated scroll box or a capped top-100 view;
- filter/search it by the same lifecycle, quality, and classification state the app and any agent use internally, so "why is this hidden from me" always has a visible answer;
- export or query a targeted slice of their own job data, not only trigger an all-or-nothing backup bundle;
- see and, where appropriate, override any automated classification or archival decision.

The exact UI and storage shape are an implementation question; the principle — the user's own data stays accessible, inspectable, and understandable — is not.

## Long-term job-market intelligence, not just noise reduction

The point of curating the pool down is not a smaller database for its own sake — it's turning a noisy scrape into something that answers real questions:

- *What should I apply to right now?*
- *What kinds of roles are actually appearing for me?*
- *Which roles repeatedly match my profile?*
- *What requirements do employers repeatedly ask for?*
- *What skills am I missing?*
- *Which job families give the best realistic opportunities?*
- *What should I learn or reposition toward to get hired faster?*

Answering these durably requires structured, persistent attributes per job beyond the raw scrape — illustrative, not a mandated schema: role family, job type, seniority, location, source, freshness, data quality, duplicate-cluster membership, application status, review/verification status, apply priority, relevant skills/requirements, detected skill gaps, and the reason a job was kept, archived, or removed. This is also why archival and deletion are not the same operation: a job moving out of the *active/operational* pool should not stop existing for this *historical/analytical* one. Whatever the lifecycle looks like, an archived/historical job should remain queryable for pattern analysis even once it's out of the working set.

## A guardrail worth stating explicitly

Relevance, data quality, duplication, freshness, actionability, and historical value are different questions. The existing single `score` (already known to be non-comparable across `ScoreSource::Keyword` vs. `Combined` — see `best_matches.rs:108-120`) should not become the one field a lifecycle decision collapses onto. A job scoring low is not evidence it's junk; a job scoring high with a `main_content_text`-fallback description is not evidence it's trustworthy. Whatever shape this takes should keep these as separate, legible signals rather than one more overloaded number.

## Non-goals for this issue

- Not proposing a specific schema, storage engine, or command set — that's for whoever implements this to choose after looking at the current architecture, including whether extending `AutopilotStore`, adding a parallel curated store, or something else fits best.
- Not asking to raise the MCP/transport payload cap.
- Not asking for score-threshold auto-deletion, or any bulk-delete path.
- Not architecting around any single AI provider — see "provider-agnostic" evidence above; the existing seam already supports this and must keep doing so.
- Not re-scoping #1167/#1168 (compact projection, server-side field filters, `applied`/`isAgency` on `found-jobs`, `best-matches` cursor) — that work makes the *existing* corpus efficient to read and is complementary; this issue is about the corpus itself never being bounded or classified in the first place.
- Not re-litigating #1146 (MCP protocol/distribution roadmap) — that's about wire-level polish and reach, orthogonal to this.
- Not scoped to any one installation's current corpus size — this is a general capability for any long-running Autopilot setup, and should hold up at corpus sizes larger than anything seen today.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A job's standing in the pool is expressed as real state, not inferred from whether it happens to still be in `found_jobs` — recoverable at every transition, never a silent hard delete.
- [ ] Reasoning over the pool (clustering, ranking, classification) no longer costs O(everything ever discovered) on every call as the pool grows — cost scales with the active/working set, not lifetime history.
- [ ] The existing dedup/cluster engine, the resume skill-gap engine, the shared AI-provider config, and the `rerank.rs` cost-safe batch pattern are reused by whatever classification/curation mechanism ships — not reimplemented.
- [ ] The app can run classification/curation on its own schedule, using whichever AI provider is currently configured, without a human or an external agent triggering it each time; a provider outage or budget exhaustion degrades gracefully instead of corrupting state.
- [ ] Curation/lifecycle state persists in the app's own data layer and survives a provider, model, API key, or agent-session change untouched — nothing here is owned by or reset by the AI layer.
- [ ] An agent can inspect population shape, find duplicate clusters, corrupted/thin records, and stale records, and retrieve a curated high-value subset — all through bounded/paged calls, without pulling the raw corpus and without the transport cap changing.
- [ ] An agent (or the GUI) can request repair, reclassification, or an archive/restore transition on a specific record, and see the reason a record is in its current state.
- [ ] The human user can see, filter, and export the full corpus and its curation state — not only an unpaginated per-autopilot list, a capped top-100, or an all-or-nothing backup bundle.
- [ ] Nothing here requires a bigger MCP payload cap, and nothing here deletes data outright.
- [ ] Historical/archived jobs remain queryable for pattern analysis (companies, role families, requirement trends) even once they're out of the active operational pool.
- [ ] Works incrementally — a newly-discovered job gets evaluated on its own, not by re-running classification over the entire accumulated history.

## Related (not duplicates — read and cross-checked before filing, re-checked before this revision)

- #1115, #1129, #1135, #1130 (closed) — fixed the transport-side symptom (no pagination existed at all). This issue is about the corpus those pages read from.
- #1167, #1168 (open, already scheduled per maintainer comment) — make the *existing* unbounded corpus efficiently queryable (compact rows, server-side filters, title/company search, `applied`/`isAgency` flags, `best-matches` cursor). Complementary: that work is about *reading* what's there; this issue is about the corpus never being bounded, classified, or given a lifecycle in the first place.
- #1146 (open) — MCP protocol/distribution roadmap (tool metadata, elicitation, `.mcpb` bundling, registry listing). Different axis entirely (wire-level/reach), not pool architecture.
- #1105, #1114/#1117 (closed/shipped) — fixed honest score/trust signaling for missing descriptions, then added automatic enrichment. Directly relevant as evidence above (the enrichment fallback's corruption risk), but neither touches pool lifecycle or bounding.
- #1172, #1173 (open, filed after this issue) — MCP transport/registration surface (loopback Streamable HTTP, generic client docs). Orthogonal: about how a client connects to the server, not about the job data the server serves.
